title: Specific heat capacity: why water takes so long to heat up
examples: Why does water take so long to boil?
How do you calculate energy to heat water?

items.label: Copper
items.ask: Why do metals heat up so quickly?

explain.say: At the beach in Goa at midday, the sand burns your feet, yet the sea feels cool. Both got the same sunshine! Why the difference? Water needs lots of energy to warm up. We measure that with specific heat capacity.

draw.text: Specific heat capacity: why water takes so long to heat up

items.label: Copper
items.ask: Why do metals heat up so quickly?

explain.say: Look at the tallest bar: water, 4200. That means it takes 4200 joules to warm 1 kilogram of water by just 1 degree. That number is its specific heat capacity: energy per kilogram per degree. Is water's bar the biggest?

items.label: Copper
items.ask: Why do metals heat up so quickly?

explain.say: Yes, by far! Now look at the short bar for copper: only 385 joules for the same 1 degree. So copper heats up about ten times faster than water with the same energy. That is why a metal pan gets hot long before the water in it. Which heats fastest here?

items.label: Copper
items.ask: Why do metals heat up so quickly?

explain.say: Copper, well done! Now this graph is for 1 kilogram of water. Every 4.2 kilojoules raises it 1 degree, so the line climbs steadily. The rule is energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature rise. See the dot at 8.4 kilojoules? What rise does it give?

marks.label: 4.2 kJ: +1 °C
marks.ask: How do you calculate the energy needed to heat water?

explain.say: 2 degrees, perfect! Wow fact: because the oceans store so much heat, coastal cities like Lisbon and Mumbai have milder weather than inland places. Challenge: how much energy warms 2 kilograms of water by 10 degrees? Hint: 2 times 4200 times 10.

marks.label: 4.2 kJ: +1 °C
marks.ask: How do you calculate the energy needed to heat water?

faq.a: It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 degree Celsius. For water it is about 4200 joules.

faq.q: Why do metals heat up so quickly?
faq.a: Metals have a low specific heat capacity, so a small amount of energy raises their temperature a lot.
asks: Why does a metal pan get hot fast?

faq.q: How do you calculate the energy needed to heat water?
faq.a: Use energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change. For 1 kilogram of water warmed by 10 degrees, that is 42 000 joules.

faq.q: Why does the sea stay cool when sand is hot?
faq.a: Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than sand, so the same sunshine warms it far less.
asks: Why is sand hotter than sea?

faq.q: Why is water used in radiators and car engines?
faq.a: Its high specific heat capacity lets it carry and store lots of heat without getting too hot.
asks: Why is water a good coolant?

facts: The specific heat capacity of water is about 4200 J/kg°C.
Change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.
